title: How Security Buyers Can Evaluate a Tool Before a Proof of Concept
summary: How security buyers can evaluate a tool before a proof of concept, with no agent installed or environment connected. A presales playbook from Storylane.
body_markdown:
Here is the position I will defend: in security sales, the proof of concept is too expensive to be the first time a buyer touches your product. A security POC usually means a deployed agent, a connected cloud account, an SSO integration or a log pipeline, and a security review before any of that can happen. If the buyer has not already convinced themselves that your tool fits their problem, the POC becomes the evaluation, and your sales engineers end up running weeks of technical work for buyers who were never going to buy.


The fix is not to skip the POC. Security buyers will always want to see the tool against their own data before they sign. The fix is to give them a credible way to evaluate the product **before** anything gets installed, so the POC is reserved for buyers who have already decided the tool is worth the effort.


I'm Madhav, CMO at Storylane. This piece is written for sales engineers and presales leaders at security vendors. It is not a general guide to running proofs of concept (we have one:[our guide to running a sales POC](https://www.storylane.io/blog/sales-poc) ). It covers the stage before that: how a security buyer can evaluate your tool without installing an agent or connecting their environment, and how presales can use that stage to qualify who gets a POC.


## Short answer: how can security buyers evaluate a tool before a proof of concept?


Security buyers can evaluate a tool before a proof of concept in four ways that need nothing from their environment:


- **A self-guided interactive demo** of the core workflow (for example, triaging an alert, investigating an identity, or reviewing a cloud misconfiguration), so they see how the product actually behaves rather than how the slides describe it.
- **A free-roam sandbox demo** populated with realistic but fake data, so technical evaluators can click anywhere, open the settings, and check the depth of the product on their own time.
- **Documentation and security artifacts** (architecture, data flow, deployment model, compliance reports) so the security and procurement reviewers can start their own track early.
- **A scoped technical session** with a sales engineer, where the buyer's questions drive the walkthrough and the success criteria for a possible POC get written down.


None of these require an agent, an API key, or a read-only role in the buyer's cloud. Together they answer the question every security buyer has before a POC: is this tool worth the cost of testing?


## Why the pre-POC stage matters more in security than anywhere else


Most B2B software can be trialed with a login and a CSV import. Security tools rarely can. To show real value, an endpoint product needs an agent on machines, a cloud security product needs access to cloud accounts, an identity product needs a connection to the directory, and a detection product needs telemetry flowing in. Every one of those steps touches production systems that the buyer's own security team is paid to protect.


That creates three costs that other categories do not carry:


- **Internal approval cost.** Before a vendor agent goes on a single laptop, the buyer often has to get sign-off from IT, the change advisory process, and sometimes legal. Your champion spends political capital just to start the test.
- **Security review cost.** The buyer will usually want to review the vendor before granting access. That is a reasonable request, and it is also why[security questionnaires land on presales desks](https://www.storylane.io/blog/security-questionnaire-presales) earlier than anyone planned.
- **Sales engineering cost.** Your SE scopes the test, helps with deployment, tunes the configuration so the results are not noisy, and then walks the buyer through findings. That is time that cannot go to another deal.


When all three costs are paid by a buyer who was only curious, everyone loses. The buyer burns goodwill internally, and the vendor burns its scarcest resource: experienced SE hours.


## What "evaluate without installing anything" actually means


A pre-POC evaluation is not a watered-down trial. It is a different question. A POC answers "does this work in our environment?" A pre-POC evaluation answers "is this the right kind of tool, built the right way, for the problem we have?"


Those are separable. A buyer can learn a great deal about a security tool without connecting it to anything:


What the buyer wants to know Needs their environment? Best pre-POC way to answer it


What does the analyst workflow look like day to day? No Interactive demo of the core workflow


How deep are the investigation, policy and reporting screens? No Free-roam sandbox demo with realistic data


How is the product deployed, and what data leaves our network? No Architecture and data flow documentation, SE session


Does the vendor meet our security and compliance bar? No Trust documentation and security questionnaire


Will it detect or catch what matters in our estate? Yes The POC itself


What is the false positive load on our real data? Yes The POC itself


Does it integrate cleanly with our existing stack? Usually yes The POC, scoped from questions raised earlier


Look at the split. Most of the questions that decide whether a tool is even a fit can be answered without touching the buyer's systems. Only the last few, the ones about real-world performance, need the POC. That is exactly what the POC should be for.


## The old way versus the better way


In a lot of security sales teams, the sequence looks like this: discovery call, slide deck, live demo on a shared demo tenant, then "let's set up a POC." The POC is offered early because it feels like the strongest closing tool, and because buyers in this category are trained to ask for one.


The problem is that the live demo is the only product exposure before the POC, and it is controlled entirely by the vendor. The buyer's technical evaluators, the analysts and engineers who will actually use the tool, often were not on that call. They meet the product for the first time during the POC, which means the POC becomes a learning exercise rather than a validation exercise.


Stage The old way The better way


First product exposure Live demo, vendor driving, champion only Interactive demo sent to the whole evaluation group


Technical depth check Happens inside the POC Sandbox demo the analysts explore on their own time


Security review of the vendor Starts when access is requested Starts in parallel, before the POC is scoped


POC scope Broad, "let's see what it finds" Narrow, built from questions the pre-POC stage raised


Who gets a POC Anyone who asks Buyers who engaged with the pre-POC evaluation


If your team is debating whether the buyer needs a proof of concept or a proof of value,[this breakdown of POC vs POV](https://www.storylane.io/blog/poc-vs-pov) covers that choice. The pre-POC stage sits before both, and it makes either one shorter.


## Interactive demos versus sandbox demos for security evaluation


These two formats do different jobs, and security sales needs both.


### Interactive demos: the guided story


An[interactive demo](https://www.storylane.io/interactive-demos) is a clickable capture of your product with a guided path. The buyer clicks through a specific workflow with short annotations explaining what they are seeing. For security tools, the best guided demos follow one realistic scenario end to end: an alert fires, the analyst investigates, the root cause is found, the response is taken, the report is generated.


Guided demos work for the people who need the "why" more than the "how": the security leader, the economic buyer, the champion who has to explain the tool internally. They are short, they can be forwarded, and they make the case without an SE on the call.


Keep them tight. In Storylane's own analysis of marketing demos (a small sample: 34 demos and 5,409 demo sessions across 9 industries), the bottom three industries by completion rate were Cloud Computing, Cyber Security and Data Tech, which averaged 43 steps and a 10.7% completion rate. The top three averaged 11 steps and 41% completion. That analysis covered website demos rather than presales demos, so treat it as directional, but the lesson travels:[security demos tend to run long](https://www.storylane.io/blog/learnings-from-analyzing-demo-lengths-across-9-industries) , and long demos lose people. Split a big product into separate flows rather than one 40-step tour.


### Sandbox demos: the free-roam check


A[sandbox demo](https://www.storylane.io/sandbox-demo) is a working clone of the product that the buyer can click through freely, rather than following a fixed path. The hands-on evaluators want this. A detection engineer wants to open the rule editor. A SOC analyst wants to pivot from an alert to the asset to the user. An IT admin wants to see the policy settings and the reporting options. They want to check that the depth is real, not that the happy path works.


A sandbox answers that without a tenant, without credentials to a live demo environment, and without risk that a buyer changes a setting that breaks the next SE's demo. It is also safe in a way a shared demo tenant often is not: the data is fabricated, so there is no real customer data to worry about.


Interactive (guided) demo Sandbox (free-roam) demo


Primary audience Security leader, champion, economic buyer Analysts, engineers, admins


Question it answers Why this tool, and what is the workflow? Is the depth real, and how does it feel to use?


Length Short, one scenario per flow Open-ended, buyer sets the pace


When to send After discovery, before the technical session Before or after the technical session, before the POC


Signal it gives presales Who engaged and how far they got Which areas technical evaluators explored


For a deeper look at how security buyers split by role, see[our guide to interactive demos for cybersecurity sales engineers](https://www.storylane.io/blog/interactive-demos-cybersecurity-sales-engineers) .


## Using the pre-POC stage to qualify who gets a POC


This is the part most security vendors miss. A pre-POC evaluation is not only a buyer convenience. It is a qualification filter that runs without SE time.


When you send a demo link instead of scheduling another call, you learn things from what the buyer does with it:


- **Did it spread?** A demo that is opened by several people at the buyer's company suggests a real evaluation group. A demo opened once by the person you sent it to suggests a solo researcher.
- **Did the technical people go deep?** If the sandbox shows time spent in the investigation, policy or integration areas, the hands-on evaluators are doing their homework. If nobody went past the first screen, a POC will likely stall for the same reason.
- **Did questions come back?** Specific questions after a self-guided evaluation ("can we scope by business unit?", "how does the agent handle offline machines?") are a strong sign of intent, and they are your POC success criteria in waiting.
- **Did the security review start?** A buyer who asks for your trust documentation before the POC is planning for procurement. A buyer who has not thought about it yet is earlier than they appear.


From there, a simple rule helps: **no POC without engagement in the pre-POC stage, and no POC without written success criteria.** If the evaluation group has not looked at the product on their own, offer a technical session instead of a POC. That keeps the door open without committing weeks of SE time.


## An illustrative worked example


*The numbers below are hypothetical and exist only to show the math. They are not Storylane data or benchmarks.*


Imagine a security vendor whose presales team of four SEs runs POCs that each take around 25 hours of SE time across scoping, deployment help, tuning and the readout. Suppose that, today, the team runs 10 POCs a quarter, and 3 of those convert to closed deals. That is 250 SE hours a quarter, or about 83 hours per win.


Now suppose the team introduces a pre-POC stage: every buyer who asks for a POC first gets a guided demo, a sandbox link and the trust documentation, followed by a scoped technical session. Say only 6 of the original 10 buyers engage enough to qualify, and because those 6 arrive with written success criteria, each POC takes 20 hours instead of 25. If the same 3 deals still close (the buyers who were going to buy were the ones who engaged), the team spends 120 hours on POCs instead of 250, about 40 hours per win.


Two caveats keep this honest. First, the pre-POC stage costs some time of its own (building and maintaining the demos, running the technical sessions), so the saving is smaller than the raw POC math suggests. Second, some buyers who would have bought may drop out if the process feels like a hurdle. That is why the pre-POC stage must be faster and easier than the POC, not an extra gate. Measure your own numbers before and after, rather than trusting any example, including this one.


## What to put in a pre-POC security evaluation kit


A practical kit for a security product usually includes:


1. **One guided demo per core use case.** For example: alert triage, investigation, policy configuration, reporting. Keep each one short and scenario based.
2. **A sandbox demo of the analyst console.** Populated with realistic, fabricated data that looks lived-in: real-looking hostnames, users, alerts, and timelines. An empty console tells the buyer nothing.
3. **A deployment and architecture overview.** What gets installed, where data is processed, what permissions the product needs. This is what the buyer's own security team will ask first.
4. **Your trust and compliance documentation** , ready to send before anyone asks.
5. **A draft POC success criteria template** the buyer fills in after the evaluation. If they cannot fill it in, they are not ready for a POC.


Keep the kit consistent across the team. When every SE builds their own version, buyers get uneven experiences, and you lose the ability to compare engagement across deals.


## Where Storylane Demo Suite fits (full disclosure)


Storylane makes interactive and sandbox demos, so I have an interest here. With that said, this is what the product does that is relevant to a pre-POC security evaluation, as described on our own product pages today:


- **Sandbox demos built from HTML captures.** You click through your product once, and Storylane captures the screens as working HTML with buttons linked, so buyers can roam the product freely. Sandbox demos are built on HTML recordings and require the Growth plan or above; screenshot-based interactive demos are available on all plans, including free.
- **Realistic demo data without real customer data.** You can blur sensitive data and use AI to replace real records with generated data, so the sandbox looks lived-in without exposing anything real. For security vendors, that matters: you are not putting a customer's alerts in front of a prospect.
- **Access controls on the demo itself.** Demos can be secured by password, expiry or email domain, which is useful when you only want a specific buyer's evaluation group to open the link.
- **Engagement analytics.** Storylane tracks engagement, completion, time spent and drop-offs, and can connect demo sessions to open deals in HubSpot or Salesforce. That is the signal you use to decide who is ready for a POC.
- **Presenter mode for live sessions.** When the scoped technical session happens, the SE can run the same sandbox live with private notes the buyer cannot see.
- **Enterprise security posture.** Storylane is SOC 2 Type II certified, GDPR compliant, and supports SSO and SAML 2.0, per our enterprise page.


What Storylane is not: it is not a replacement for the POC. A sandbox demo shows how your product behaves with fabricated data. It cannot show how your detection logic performs on a buyer's real telemetry. Use it to qualify and prepare buyers for the POC, then run the POC on their environment.


## How to measure whether the pre-POC stage is working


Pick a small set of numbers and track them per quarter, using your CRM as the source of truth:


Metric What it tells you Which direction you want


POC-to-close rate Whether POCs are going to the right buyers Up


SE hours per POC Whether buyers arrive with clearer scope Down


Days from POC start to decision Whether the POC validates rather than educates Down


Share of POC requests that pass the pre-POC stage How strict your filter is Stable, not near zero


Win rate on deals that skipped the pre-POC stage Whether the filter is losing good buyers Watch it, do not ignore it


Read these with care. Small presales teams run few POCs a quarter, so one or two deals can swing the rate a lot. Look at the trend over several quarters, and compare deals that went through the pre-POC stage with those that did not, rather than reading a single quarter as proof.


## Common mistakes


- **Making the pre-POC stage a gate the buyer resents.** If it feels like a hoop, buyers will route around it or go to a competitor who will give them a POC immediately. Frame it as "here is the fastest way for your team to see whether this is worth testing."
- **Sending an empty sandbox.** A console with no alerts and no assets says nothing about the product. Fill it with realistic, fabricated data.
- **One giant demo.** Security products are deep, and it is tempting to show everything. Split by use case and by role.
- **Ignoring the engagement data.** Sending demos and never looking at who opened them wastes the best qualification signal you have.
- **Letting the demo drift from the product.** If the sandbox shows last year's UI, technical evaluators will notice, and trust drops. Update the screens that change with each release.
- **Treating the demo as proof of detection.** Never imply that a sandbox shows how the tool will perform on the buyer's data. Security buyers will catch it, and it damages credibility.


## The bottom line


Security POCs are expensive for both sides, and that will not change, because the buyer needs proof on their own systems before they sign. What can change is who gets one. Give security buyers a real way to evaluate the tool before anything gets installed: guided demos for the people who need the story, sandbox demos for the people who need the depth, documentation for the people who need to review you. Then use what they do with it to decide who is ready for a POC. Your SEs will spend their hours on the deals that can close, and your POCs will be shorter, sharper and easier to win.

## FAQ


### How can security buyers evaluate a tool before a proof of concept?


They can use a self-guided interactive demo of the core workflow, a free-roam sandbox demo with realistic fabricated data, the vendor's architecture and trust documentation, and a scoped technical session with a sales engineer. None of these require installing an agent or connecting the buyer's environment.


### Can a sandbox demo replace a security POC?


No. A sandbox demo shows how the product works with fabricated data. It cannot show how detection or protection performs on the buyer's real systems and telemetry. Use it to qualify buyers and scope the POC, not to replace it.


### Who should get a POC in security sales?


Buyers whose evaluation group has engaged with the pre-POC material, who can write down specific success criteria, and who have started (or are ready to start) a security review of the vendor. Buyers who have not looked at the product on their own are usually better served by a technical session first.


### What should a pre-POC security evaluation kit include?


One short guided demo per core use case, a sandbox demo of the analyst console with realistic data, a deployment and architecture overview, the vendor's trust and compliance documentation, and a POC success criteria template.


### Is it safe to share a sandbox demo of a security product?


It can be, if the sandbox uses fabricated data rather than real customer data and access is controlled. In Storylane, demos can be secured by password, expiry or email domain, and sensitive data can be blurred or replaced with generated data.
